title: Pulmonary Acinus & Alveoli Anatomy: Gas-Exchange Guides
description: Explore pulmonary acinus and alveoli microanatomy, detailing respiratory bronchioles, Type I and Type II pneumocytes, surfactant, and gas-exchange barrier.
h1: Pulmonary Acinus and Alveoli Anatomy: Pneumocytes and Blood-Air Barrier
blurb: Inside the terminal respiratory unit: flat Type I pneumocytes, surfactant-secreting Type II cells, alveolar macrophages, and the 0.5-micron blood-air barrier.
lead: At the terminal tips of the bronchial tree, roughly 300 to 500 million microscopic air sacs create a gas-exchange surface area nearly the size of a tennis court. In this illustrated guide to pulmonary acinus and alveoli, we examine 20 documented structures—including terminal bronchiole, respiratory bronchiole, alveolar duct, alveolar sac—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: At the terminal tips of the bronchial tree, roughly 300 to 500 million microscopic air sacs create a gas-exchange surface area nearly the size of a tennis court. A terminal bronchiole is the last purely conducting airway. Its distal respiratory bronchioles bear occasional alveoli and lead to alveolar ducts, sacs and alveoli. Thin type I pneumocytes cover most air-exchange surface; type II cells secrete surfactant and can contribute to epithelial repair. The air–blood barrier includes alveolar epithelium, thin interstitium/fused basement membranes and capillary endothelium. Alveolar macrophages provide immune surveillance; capillary red cells pass closely alongside exchange surfaces. Within the human body, the pulmonary acinus · gas-exchange barrier (Acinus pulmonis · alveoli) is situated in distal to a terminal bronchiole within secondary pulmonary lobules, receives arterial perfusion via pulmonary arterioles → alveolar capillaries → pulmonary venules; bronchial arteries supply conducting tissue, and is innervated by autonomic fibers to airways/vessels; alveolar wall is not a skeletal-muscle structure.

Structurally, the terminal bronchiole (Bronchiolus terminalis) comprises final nonalveolated conducting airway before respiratory zone. Physiologically, the terminal bronchiole delivers air to downstream acinus. Structurally, the respiratory bronchiole (Bronchiolus respiratorius) comprises first airway segment with alveoli interrupting its wall. Physiologically, the respiratory bronchiole governs combines air conduction and some gas exchange. Structurally, the alveolar duct (Ductus alveolaris) comprises distal passage whose walls are largely alveolar openings. Physiologically, the alveolar duct distributes air to multiple alveolar sacs. Structurally, the alveolar sac (Sacculus alveolaris) comprises common terminal chamber opening into a cluster of alveoli. Physiologically, the alveolar sac governs shares airflow among terminal alveoli. The alveolus (Alveolus pulmonis) is tiny airspace lined by specialized epithelium and surrounded by capillaries. Physiologically, the alveolus provides extensive diffusion surface. Structurally, the type I pneumocyte (Pneumocytus typus I) comprises very thin squamous alveolar epithelial cell covering most alveolar surface. Physiologically, the type I pneumocyte governs minimizes gas diffusion distance.

Clinically, the terminal bronchiole contains no cartilage plates or submucosal glands. Clinically, the respiratory bronchiole marks proximal boundary of acinus. In clinical pathology involving the alveolar duct, more extensively alveolated than respiratory bronchiole. Medical evaluation of the alveolar sac also notes that not synonymous with a single alveolus.

questions.question: What is a pulmonary acinus?
questions.answer: An acinus is the lung region distal to a terminal bronchiole where respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli participate in gas exchange. It is a microanatomical unit, not a whole lung lobe.

questions.question: How do Type I and Type II alveolar cells differ?
questions.answer: Type I pneumocytes are thin squamous lining cells specialized for gas exchange. Type II pneumocytes are plumper cells that make surfactant and help replenish the alveolar lining.

questions.question: What is the alveolar–capillary barrier?
questions.answer: It is the thin interface separating air in an alveolus from blood in a nearby capillary, involving alveolar epithelium, shared basement membranes and capillary endothelium. Its short diffusion distance supports gas exchange.

questions.question: Are alveolar macrophages attached to the wall?
questions.answer: Alveolar macrophages can move on the air-facing surface of alveoli and engulf inhaled particles and debris. They are not the same as Type I or Type II epithelial cells.

questions.question: Is the Type I cell image a histology photograph?
questions.answer: No. It is a digital teaching illustration of an alveolar cell, not a tissue specimen or clinical slide.
